text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNFollow electron–ion temperature differences using energy conservation, and distinguish exchange and flow times. Connect to foundations: Stars, gas, vacuum, and the forces of nature ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01A gas need not have just one temperature Temperature measures random particle motion. Electrons and protons can each have a thermal distribution while having different temperatures. A temperature for each species already assumes internal thermalization; it does not require that the two species have finished exchanging energy with each other. A collisionless shock can leave different species with different shares of the thermal energy. Supply the initial ratio β = Tₑ₀/Tᵢ₀ rather than deriving it from the total jump conditions. Then isolate subsequent Coulomb energy exchange from the much more complicated shock heating process. Assume fully ionized pure hydrogen with nₑ = nᵢ = n, nonrelativistic particles, fixed density and volume. Omit external heating, radiation losses, and expansion. 02Energy gained by one species is lost by the other uₑ=32nkBTₑ, uᵢ=32nkBTᵢ Qₑᵢ=32nkBTᵢ−Tₑtₑᵢ Qₑᵢ is energy received by electrons per volume per time and is positive when ions are hotter. The ions lose exactly that amount. Equal number densities give equal heat capacities, so the two temperature equations have opposite right-hand sides. Adding them checks conservation before any numerical calculation. dTₑdt=Tᵢ−Tₑtₑᵢ, dTᵢdt=−Tᵢ−Tₑtₑᵢ Tₑ+Tᵢ=Tₑ₀+Tᵢ₀, T̄=Tₑ₀+Tᵢ₀2 03Exponential relaxation and the factor of two Subtract the electron equation from the ion equation. Cooling of ions and heating of electrons both reduce the difference Δ = Tᵢ−Tₑ. For a constant exchange time τ, separation of variables gives a simple benchmark. dΔdt=−2Δτ ⇒ dΔΔ=−2dtτ Δ=Δ₀e−2t/τ, Tₑ=T̄−Δ2, Tᵢ=T̄+Δ2 Here τ is the exchange time in the electron equation; the difference has an e-folding time τ/2. Holding ions at a prescribed temperature would instead describe an external heat reservoir. Checking which temperatures are allowed to change prevents a factor-of-two error. 04Supply the collision time and follow relaxation Supply the standard exchange time for a weakly coupled classical plasma. In the SI formula below, use density in m⁻³, temperatures in K, and charge in coulombs. Fix the dimensionless Coulomb logarithm at 30 instead of deriving the collision integral. tₑᵢ=3mₑmₚ8√(2π) n [e²/(4πε₀)]² lnΛ (kBTₑmₑ+kBTᵢmₚ)3/2 When the electron thermal-speed term dominates, tₑᵢ scales as Tₑ³ᐟ²/n. Heating electrons then slows exchange, so the panel updates the coefficient rather than using a single exponential. Labels in keV mean kBT, an energy representation of temperature; 1 keV corresponds to about 1.16 × 10⁷ K. Numerically integrate dt/dy = tₑᵢ/2 with y = ln(Δ₀/Δ), then invert the cumulative time. Simpson integration and local bisection give the temperatures while their sum is preserved analytically. The difference stays positive, and equal initial temperatures remain equal. 05Choose the relevant competing clock Compare the flow residence time with the near-equilibrium difference-decay time tₑᵢ(T̄)/2. A long exchange clock permits a difference to survive passage through the region. Since the coefficient changes during relaxation, inspect the trajectory as well as the single clock ratio. The panel is a closed parcel calculation, not a simulated flow. Its residence time is an external comparison scale. Maintaining two temperatures indefinitely requires sources or sinks that distinguish species; exchange alone eventually produces one temperature. Connect to heating in shocks and particle acceleration and electron pressure in the SZ effect. Total pressure is nkB(Tₑ+Tᵢ), whereas the electron pressure is nkBTₑ. Equal total energy therefore does not guarantee equal electron-pressure signals. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. For equal electron and proton densities and constant exchange time τ, does the temperature difference fall by e in τ or τ/2? Show the answer and reasoning Both temperatures change, so d(Tᵢ−Tₑ)/dt = −2(Tᵢ−Tₑ)/τ. The difference decays in τ/2, unlike a model with externally fixed ion temperature.
